title: State of Nevada v. Duane Davis
phase: Both sides rested — closing arguments Monday, Aug. 31
charges: One count of murder with use of a deadly weapon, charged with a criminal-gang enhancement — the state alleges the killing was done "knowingly for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in affiliation with" a criminal gang.
defendant: Duane Keith "Keffe D" Davis, 63, of Henderson, Nevada
plea: Not guilty — the defense says every word linking Davis to the shooting came out of Davis's own mouth, told for book sales and attention, and that no independent evidence backs any of it up.
prosecution: Binu Palal, Chief Deputy District Attorney
Marc DiGiacomo, Chief Deputy District Attorney
plainSummary: Tupac Shakur was 25 when someone in a white Cadillac fired into his car on a Las Vegas side street in September 1996. He died six days later, and for nearly thirty years nobody was charged. Duane "Keffe D" Davis is on trial now because of the one thing that finally cracked the case open: his own mouth. The jury's question is not really who was in that Cadillac — it is whether a man's own confessions, sold in a memoir and repeated on camera for years, are enough to convict him when almost everyone who could confirm or deny them is dead.
statusNow: The prosecution rested on Aug. 26, 2026 after eight days of testimony and roughly two dozen witnesses, having built its case largely on Davis's own recorded and published accounts of the 1996 killing. On Aug. 27 the defense presented three witnesses — two LVMPD officers who were on duty near Suge Knight's home the night of the shooting and a former homicide detective who testified that no tested firearm matched the crime-scene casings — and rested the same day; Davis waived his right to testify and prosecutors declined to call rebuttal witnesses. After a charge conference on Friday, Aug. 28, closing arguments to the 12 jurors and four alternates are set for Monday, Aug. 31, after which the jury begins deliberating. If convicted, Davis faces a possible life sentence.
storySoFar: On September 7, 1996, Tupac Shakur and Death Row Records boss Suge Knight watched Mike Tyson fight at the MGM Grand. In the lobby afterwards, Shakur and his entourage beat a young Compton man named Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, and casino cameras caught it. About two and a half hours later a white Cadillac pulled alongside Knight's BMW near the Strip and someone inside opened fire; Shakur, 25, died six days later and the case went cold for decades. Then Anderson's uncle — former South Side Compton Crips leader Duane "Keffe D" Davis — published a 2019 memoir describing how he rode in that Cadillac and passed a gun into the back seat, and spent years repeating versions of the story on camera. Police reopened the file, searched a Henderson home tied to Davis in July 2023, and a Clark County grand jury indicted him that September. Prosecutors say the man who talked his way into a book deal talked his way into a murder charge. Davis says he made the whole thing up to sell books, and his lawyer says nothing independent of Davis's own words connects him to the shooting.

livestream.note: The trial is being carried gavel-to-gavel. 8 News Now (KLAS, Las Vegas) streams every minute from its dedicated trial page, and Fox 5 Vegas and News 3 Las Vegas both run live courtroom feeds while court is in session; Court TV is also covering it daily. Court resumes Monday, August 24 at 9:30 a.m. Pacific.

verdictOptions.option: Guilty of first-degree murder, gang finding true
verdictOptions.consequence: Davis waived his right to have the jury decide his sentence, so Judge Kierny would pick from three options for the murder itself: life with no chance of parole, life with a first parole hearing after 20 years, or a flat 50 years with parole possible after 20. On top of that she could add 1 to 20 years for using a deadly weapon and another 1 to 20 years for the gang finding, both served after the murder term. At 63, any of those realistically means Davis dies in prison.

verdictOptions.option: Guilty of first-degree murder, but jurors reject the gang claim
verdictOptions.consequence: Same three sentencing options for the murder, plus the weapon add-on, but the extra 1-to-20-year gang term drops away. The state has to prove the gang allegation beyond a reasonable doubt, separately from the murder itself — jurors can believe he did it and still say the state did not prove it was gang business.

This is the lesser option — a killing without the planning and deliberation first-degree murder requires. It carries life with parole possible after 10 years, or 25 years with parole possible after 10, plus the weapon add-on. Whether jurors actually get this choice depends on the final instructions Judge Kierny reads them at the end of the case.

Davis walks out of the Regional Justice Center a free man for the first time since September 2023, and can never be tried again for Tupac Shakur's killing. An acquittal cannot be appealed by the state.
If jurors cannot all agree, Judge Kierny declares a mistrial and nothing is decided. The District Attorney's office can then choose to try the whole case again in front of a new jury, or drop it.

legalStandard.name: Can a confession alone convict? Nevada's corroboration rule
legalStandard.test: Nevada still follows the old "corpus delicti" rule — Latin for "body of the crime." The Nevada Supreme Court has put it plainly: "The corpus delicti must be demonstrated by evidence independent of the confessions or admissions of the defendant," a rule that "protects against an accused's conviction being based solely upon an uncorroborated confession." Here, that a crime happened is not in dispute: a medical examiner told jurors Tupac Shakur was shot and that "the manner of death was homicide." The real fight is the next step — whether anything that does not come out of Duane Davis's mouth actually ties Davis to that shooting. A separate Nevada rule, NRS 175.291, does the same job for accomplices: if a witness could have been charged with the same crime, a jury cannot convict on that witness's word alone unless other evidence "tends to connect the defendant with the commission of the offense," and evidence that merely shows the crime happened is not enough.
legalStandard.burden: The State carries the whole load. Prosecutors must prove every element of murder beyond a reasonable doubt, and must separately prove the gang allegation beyond a reasonable doubt for the extra penalty to apply. Davis does not have to prove anything, does not have to testify, and his silence cannot be held against him. The defense strategy is built entirely on the state's burden: not "here is what really happened," but "you have nothing but his own talk."

qa.q: Davis described the shooting himself. Why isn’t that enough to convict him?
qa.a: Nevada’s corpus delicti rule says a conviction cannot rest on an uncorroborated confession. In a killing, the state has to prove with evidence that did not come out of the defendant’s mouth that there was a death, and that the death came about through the criminal act of another person. The Nevada Supreme Court set out both halves in Sheriff v. Dhadda, and explained the reason plainly: confessions get misreported, coerced, misremembered, or made by people who are not well.

qa.q: So does the state need independent proof that Davis himself was there?
qa.a: Not under that rule, and this is the part most readers get wrong. Corpus delicti covers the fact of the killing, not who did it. The rule that does the identity work in this trial is NRS 175.291. Where a witness could have been charged with the same crime, a jury cannot convict on that witness’s word alone unless other evidence “tends to connect the defendant with the commission of the offense”, and the statute says evidence that merely shows the offence happened does not count.

It does not have to prove guilt by itself. In Gallego v. State the Nevada Supreme Court upheld a conviction on the cumulative weight of circumstantial items, among them uncommon rope matching what bound the victims and proof the defendant was in Nevada around the time. Taken together they tended to tie him to the killings, and that is the test. Corroboration can be circumstantial and it can be modest, so long as it points at this defendant rather than only at the crime.
